title: Inter-spike intervals of a Poisson neuron, with and without a refractory period
promptMarkdown:
Model a neuron as a homogeneous Poisson process with rate $r$: in every short interval $dt$ a spike occurs with probability $r\,dt$, independently of the past. This is a descriptive model; nothing here is a recording.

1. Derive the probability density of the inter-spike interval $\tau$, its mean and its standard deviation, and hence the coefficient of variation CV.
2. Now add an absolute refractory period: after each spike no spike can occur for a time $t_{ref}$, after which the process resumes at rate $r$. Derive the new ISI density, mean, standard deviation and CV, and show that CV $< 1$.
3. For $r = 20\ \text{s}^{-1}$ and $t_{ref} = 5$ ms, compute the mean ISI in ms and the CV.
4. W1D1 Tutorial 1 fits candidate functions to ISI histograms from the Steinmetz et al. (2019) recordings. Name two features of a recorded ISI histogram that would refute the pure Poisson model, and one that the refractory model would also fail to capture. Say in one sentence why a good fit of the exponential form would not show that the neuron 'is' a Poisson process.
hintLadder: Let $S(\tau)$ be the probability that no spike has occurred in $(0, \tau]$ after a spike at 0. Independence gives $S(\tau + dt) = S(\tau)(1 - r\,dt)$; turn this into a differential equation.
The density is $-dS/d\tau$. Mean and variance of the exponential follow from $\int_0^\infty \tau^k r e^{-r\tau}\,d\tau = k!/r^k$.
With a refractory period the interval is $t_{ref}$ plus an exponential variable: shift the density, and recall that adding a constant changes the mean but not the standard deviation.
A gap near zero, a peak at a preferred interval, or a CV far from 1 are all features the pure model cannot produce; successive-interval correlations are something neither model produces.

deterministicChecks.description: CV = 1/(1 + r t_ref) = 0.909 for the given numbers
claiming that the refractory period raises the CV or makes it exceed 1
the densities must be derived in general, not evaluated at particular values

criteria.criterion: Survival function S(τ) = e^{−rτ} derived from independence; density p(τ) = r e^{−rτ}; mean 1/r, SD 1/r, CV = 1.

criteria.criterion: Two refuting features (gap at short intervals, CV ≠ 1, peak or bimodality); one feature beyond the refractory model (serial correlations, bursts, rate non-stationarity); and the point that a fit shows shape, not mechanism or independence.

checkExamples.label: correct derivation
checkExamples.text: Let S(τ) be the probability of no spike in (0, τ]. For all τ, S(τ + dt) = S(τ)(1 − r dt), so dS/dτ = −rS and S = e^{−rτ}; the density is p(τ) = −S' = r e^{−rτ}, with mean 1/r, variance 1/r², SD 1/r and CV = 1. With a refractory period the interval is t_ref plus an exponential variable: p(τ) = r e^{−r(τ − t_ref)} for τ ≥ t_ref, mean t_ref + 1/r, SD 1/r (a shift does not change the spread), CV = (1/r)/(t_ref + 1/r) = 1/(1 + r t_ref) < 1. Numbers: mean = 5 + 50 = 55 ms, CV = 1/1.1 = 0.909. Refuting features: a gap at short intervals and a CV well below 1 refute the pure Poisson model; serial correlations between successive intervals (bursting) are beyond both. A good exponential fit only shows the histogram's shape; it does not show that spikes are independent, which is the mechanism-free assumption behind 'Poisson'.

checkExamples.label: reversed CV and no derivation
checkExamples.text: The refractory period increases the CV above 1 because spikes become more spread out. Mean ISI is 50 ms.
